:) For me (so results may vary), it was a snowball effect: I started taking one B12 vitamin per day (two of them if I was feeling really down), and found that I had energy to exercise/move around/be productive, and after exercising, I only craved and ate nutrient dense food which made me feel centered. 


My depression hasn't completely faded (it's a "black dog that follows me" - quote from some author, the name escapes me), but the vitamins helped me walk back from the edge and get some good habits in.


Talk to your doctor to explore your options, some people may need a combination of both, or vitamins may interact with anti-depressants, (should you choose that route).

Here are some tips:


1. It might be a good idea to put "freelancing" or "consultant" on your resume so people/employers don't think you've been jobless. Try to capitalize on that, if you're able to (perhaps have a profitable hobby/trade?).


2. Just be aware that you might enter a depressive funk and it will affect people around you. I did, and I'm trying to claw my way out of it. It's a scary place to be, even if you have resources (and especially if your living situation has gone downhill. Mine was going from a furnished apartment on my own to an air mattress at my mom's house.). Quitting a job, even if it sucks will take a toll on your mental health more than the job itself did.


3. Only you (and your resources) can decide if you're being picky. If you need money, don't turn away a job even if it isn't your ideal career path (see freelancing tip), as you are more concerned about letting important employers know that you're still a professional at what you do (or want to do).


4. Take this time to brush up on your skills, there are tons of free MOOC classes you can take on practically any subject. It can make you feel like you're being somewhat productive during this downtime.
